ety.text: From Old French germain, from Latin germānus, from germen (“seed, sprout, bud”). See also germane, a formal variant which has survived in specific senses. Not related to the proper noun German.

senses.d: Having the same mother and father; a full (brother or sister).
Being born to one’s blood aunt or uncle; a first (cousin).
ex:
The doubtfull wordes whereof they scan and canvas to an fro.
Which done, Prometheus sonne began by counsell wise and sage
The phrase would bee more Germaine.
Wert thou a Leopard, thou wert Germane to the Lion.
Which when his german saw, the stony feare / Ran to his hart, and all his sence dismayd […]

senses.d: An elaborate round dance, often with a waltz movement.
ex: Through the years, though, the german was replaced by new and more popular dances, but in many instances the name stayed on.

senses.d: A social party at which the german is danced.

grp.label: (cousin) born to one’s blood aunt or uncle

fr:germain.gl: german (having the same mother and father; a full (brother or sister))

ety.text: Inherited from Old French, borrowed from Latin germānus.

Learned borrowing from Latin germānus (“of siblings”), from germen (“sprout, bud”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵenh₁- (“to bear”). Doublet of irmão, which was inherited, and hermano, a borrowing from Spanish.
